Empirical Research Plan – Trade Liberalization and Brazilian Labor-Market Outcomes  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Baseline approach: Difference-in-Differences with continuous treatment intensity (“DiD-in-intensity”), complemented by an event-study and a shift-share extension.

• Source of quasi-randomness  
   – In 1991-94 Brazil unilaterally cut import tariffs. The size of the cut differed sharply across 4-digit manufacturing industries and was announced/implemented quickly, leaving little room for lobbying or anticipation at the firm level.  
• Design  
   – Compare changes in employment and wages before vs. after liberalization across industries that experienced large vs. small tariff declines.  
   – Treatment intensity = ∆Tariff_i (pre-1990 tariff minus post-1994 tariff) – a continuous measure.  
   – Firm-level outcomes are linked to their industry’s tariff change.  
• Why appropriate  
   – The reform provides exogenous, staggered variation that is orthogonal to contemporaneous firm-specific shocks.  
   – Rich panel allows difference-in-differences with unit and time fixed effects, dynamic event-study, and triple-difference across local labour-market exposure if desired.  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
   TREAT_i = –∆Tariff_i = (Tariff_i,1990 – Tariff_i,1994)  (positive values mean larger liberalization)  

Unit of observation for regressions  
   – Firm f in industry i, year t.  

Control Counterfactual  
   – Firms in industries with small or zero tariff cuts provide the counterfactual trend.  
   – In robustness checks we also construct a “low-exposure” group = industries in the bottom quartile of ∆Tariff.  

Treatment Timing  
   – Policy window: 1991 (announcement) to 1994 (full implementation).  
   – Pre-period: 1987-1990.  
   – Post-period: 1995-2000 (short-run) and 2001-2005 (long-run).  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent liberalization, high-cut and low-cut industries would have followed similar trends in employment/wages.  
   • Plausibility: Reasonable given that tariff schedules were historically unrelated to differential pre-1990 trends (to be verified with pre-trend tests).  

A2. Exogeneity of ∆Tariff: The magnitude of the cut is unrelated to contemporaneous industry shocks affecting post-1991 labour outcomes.  
   • Plausibility: Tariff changes were centrally determined and broad-based; lobbying was weak due to macro crisis.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Workers/firms in one industry are not directly affected by tariff cuts in another, aside from general equilibrium price effects.  
   • Plausibility: Some input-output spillovers exist; we will test robustness by excluding supplier/customer-intensive industries.  

A4. No Systematic Anticipation: Firms did not adjust labour outcomes before 1991 in response to expected tariff cuts.  
   • Plausibility: Sudden policy. We will check for pre-effects in −5 to −1 event years.  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent macro reforms (privatizations, stabilization plans)  
   – Add year×macro-sector fixed effects and control for industry privatization waves.  
   – Include industry-specific time-varying controls (exchange-rate exposure, inflation pass-through).  

T2. Industry-specific shocks (commodity price booms, technology changes)  
   – Include industry×time trends.  
   – Use placebo tariffs constructed from pre-reform Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) rates; coefficient should be zero.  

T3. Composition bias and reclassification of industry codes  
   – Track firms’ industry codes over time; restrict to firms that remain in the same 4-digit sector, or re-assign using majority sales rule.  
   – Weight regressions by base-year firm size to minimize entry/exit composition bias; alternatively, use worker-level panels if available.  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
###############################################################################
# 0. Packages
###############################################################################
library(data.table)  # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)      # high-dimensional fixed-effect regressions
library(ggplot2)

###############################################################################
# 1. Load data
###############################################################################
# Assume three csvs: firms.csv, tariffs.csv, industry_controls.csv
firms   <- fread("firms.csv")          # firm_id, year, ind4, employment, wage
tariffs <- fread("tariffs.csv")        # ind4, year, tariff
controls<- fread("industry_controls.csv") # ind4, year, priv_share, io_upstream

###############################################################################
# 2. Construct treatment – ∆Tariff_i
###############################################################################
# Compute pre and post average tariffs by industry
pre  <- tariffs[year %between% c(1988,1990),   .(tariff_pre  = mean(tariff)), by = ind4]
post <- tariffs[year %between% c(1993,1995),   .(tariff_post = mean(tariff)), by = ind4]
dT   <- merge(pre, post, by="ind4")
dT[, d_tariff := tariff_pre - tariff_post]     # larger values = larger cut

###############################################################################
# 3. Merge treatment into firm panel
###############################################################################
panel <- merge(firms, dT[,.(ind4, d_tariff)], by="ind4", all.x=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, controls, by=c("ind4","year"), all.x=TRUE)

###############################################################################
# 4. Create time indicators
###############################################################################
panel[, post := as.integer(year >= 1995)]      # adjust as desired
panel[, rel_year := year - 1991]               # for event study (-5,..., +10)

###############################################################################
# 5. Main DiD-in-intensity specification
###############################################################################
# Y_f,i,t = β * (d_tariff × post_t) + γ_i + δ_t + θ X_i,t + ε
feols_out <- feols(
   l_employment ~ d_tariff*post + priv_share + io_upstream |
   ind4 + year, data = panel, weights = ~ base_emp_1990, cluster = ~ ind4
)
summary(feols_out)

###############################################################################
# 6. Event-study (dynamic effects)
###############################################################################
panel[, rel_bucket := factor(rel_year)]
event <- feols(
  l_employment ~ d_tariff:rel_bucket |
  ind4 + year, data = panel, cluster = ~ ind4
)
iplot(event, ref.line = -1, xlab="Years relative to reform", ylab="β(t)")

###############################################################################
# 7. Robustness check – placebo tariffs
###############################################################################
# Placebo = tariff change 1984-1988 (no policy shock)
pre_pl  <- tariffs[year %between% c(1984,1986), .(tariff84 = mean(tariff)), by=ind4]
post_pl <- tariffs[year %between% c(1986,1988), .(tariff88 = mean(tariff)), by=ind4]
placebo <- merge(pre_pl, post_pl); placebo[, d_tariff_pl := tariff84 - tariff88]

panel <- merge(panel, placebo[,.(ind4,d_tariff_pl)], by="ind4", all.x=TRUE)

placebo_out <- feols(
   l_employment ~ d_tariff_pl*post | ind4 + year,
   data = panel, cluster = ~ ind4
)
summary(placebo_out)        # Expect coefficient ≈ 0
```

---------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Heckscher-Ohlin/Stolper-Samuelson) predicts that import-competing industries contract after trade liberalization.  

• Short-term (≤5 years):  
   – A 10 p.p. tariff cut is likely to reduce industry employment by roughly 5–7 %, and average real wages by 2–4 %.  
• Long-term (>10 years):  
   – Employment losses may partially reverse as surviving firms upgrade productivity; wage effects could dissipate or even turn slightly positive for skilled workers.  

---------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = weak)  
1. Pre-treatment parallel trends verified ................. 0.8  
2. Exogeneity of treatment intensity ........................ 0.7  
3. No important spillovers (SUTVA) .......................... 0.6  
4. Correct functional form & inference ..................... 0.9  
5. Robustness to alternative samples/specs ................. 0.9  

Average score: 0.78 – design is strong but hinges on plausibility of parallel trends and limited spillovers, both of which will be thoroughly tested.
